The proliferation of misinformation in digital media environments has been identified as perhaps one of the most significant threats to informed democratic participation in the contemporary era; the mechanisms by which false or misleading claims are disseminated and amplified through social platforms are, it must be noted, both technologically sophisticated and psychologically exploitative. It has been argued by several scholars that the algorithmic curation of content, which is designed to maximize user engagement, inadvertently creates conditions favorable to the spread of sensationalized and inaccurate information. The cognitive biases that render individuals susceptible to misinformation, including confirmation bias and the illusory truth effect, are arguably well established in the psychological literature; however, the interaction between these biases and the affordances of digital media remains insufficiently understood. It is perhaps incumbent upon researchers, platform developers, and policymakers to collaborate in the development of interventions that promote critical media literacy without infringing upon the principles of free expression that are foundational to democratic governance.
